doc_name: Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Yarumal)
text: The Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Spanish: Basílica Menor de Nuestra Señora de la Merced) is a minor basilica located in Yarumal, Colombia, and belongs to the Diocese of Santa Rosa de Osos, serving as the seat of the parish of the same name. It is dedicated to the Virgin Mary, with the Virgin of Mercy as its patron saint, and functions as the titular church of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga. Designed and constructed in the Renaissance Revival style as a larger replacement for Yarumal's original church, the project began in 1866 and faced numerous setbacks, including its high cost, the Colombian civil wars in the late nineteenth century, a partial collapse in 1890, and an earthquake in 1938, which delayed completion until 1944 when it was consecrated. During construction, the Chapel of Saint Aloysius—originally the cemetery chapel—was elevated to parish status. The basilica is rectangular and divided longitudinally into three parts, with a main façade composed of two domed towers joined by the central nave. It houses several artworks, including Nuestra Señora de la Merced, a 1798 painting of the Virgin of Mercy considered miraculous. In 1998, the Municipal Council of Yarumal declared both the basilica and the Chapel of Saint Aloysius a cultural and architectural landmark. On 12 August 1999, Pope John Paul II granted the church the title of minor basilica. Since 2000, the church has housed the remains of poet Epifanio Mejía, author of the Himno Antioqueño. Yarumal, originally named Saint Luis of Góngora, was founded in 1787 and initially had a straw chapel where priests from Santa Rosa de Osos held services. In 1790, the parish of Saint Luis of Góngora was established, later renamed to Our Lady of Mercy. By 1850, with a population of 3,000, it was clear that a larger church was needed. On 20 December 1860, Father Julián Palacio convened the townspeople to discuss the need for a new church and formed the first committee. On 15 January 1861, he proposed starting construction in April and authorized the first purchase of boards for rammed earth walls. On 5 February 1861, Gregorio Álvarez offered to work as bricklayer and project director for two reals and three pesos per day, and on the sixth, Palacio planted the first stone and began fundraising. A request for bishop’s authorization was approved on 2 March 1861, with the bishop urging organizational efficiency and the committee drafting seven regulatory chapters. The construction was financed through alms, collections, mandatory contributions, raffles, bazaars, and the sale of donated farms. On 4 July 1865, Santos Sánchez offered to direct architecture and masonry for five pesos per day but was not approved. On the same date, Policarpo Rivera donated land for free, including rights to build a shed and use mud, with the condition that it be returned after construction. Around this time, the committee hired laborers from Lime kilns in the Sepultura villages. On 25 August 1865, José María Zapata Muñoz was hired to direct architecture and masonry for four pesos per day, with the agreement to provide paintings and statues; he was later joined by Floro Hernández in 1868 and by Francisco Arroyave and Francisco Puerta on 18 July 1869. On 2 April 1866, Gregorio Álvarez began demolishing the old church, which stood on land belonging to the parish adjacent to municipal land north of Bolivar Square (now Epifanio Mejía park), with boundaries later clarified. On the same day, Palacio sent a letter to judicial vicar Valerio Antonio Jiménez requesting permission to build the Chapel of Our Lady of Carmen (now the Chapel of Saint Aloysius), which was granted on 17 April 1866. On 1 July 1866, Palacio requested to expand the chapel after the demolition of the old church, initially planning to sell the cemetery lot, but villagers instead proposed using funds to purchase land in front of the chapel to form a small square, which was approved by Monsignor Valerio Antonio Jiménez. On 14 February 1868, Pope Pius IX moved the seat of the Diocese of Antioquia to Medellín, renaming it Diocese of Medellín and Antioquia, though the Yarumal parish remained under its jurisdiction. With the chapel expanded and remodeled, Palacio requested and received approval from Bishop José Joaquín Isaza Ruíz to bless the chapel for Mass and sacraments while the main church was under construction. On 4 February 1873, the Diocese of Antioquia was restored, and Yarumal’s parish returned to its jurisdiction, with the seat in Medellín renamed simply as the Diocese of Medellín. In 1876, construction was halted due to the political–religious civil war from 1876 to 1877. On 1 September 1881, the board restarted work, contacting architect José María Zapata to begin on 1 December and hiring Manuel Antonio Misas to provide six thousand bricks for 38 pesos, though the agreement was canceled due to disagreements, with a 24-peso fine imposed. José María Zapata arrived in Yarumal in the first week of December 1881 to take charge, fulfilling his agreement with the board and with Father Aldemar Palacio (priest from 26 September 1875 to 5 August 1895). On 6 June 1884, priest Uladislao Ortiz and Marco A. Mejía requested approval to begin building the right tower, which was granted with a budget of 3,000 pesos. This marked the beginning of ongoing construction interruptions due to unrest, financial difficulties, and the urgent need to build a bridge over the Nechí River. On 18 June 1889, Bishop Jesús María Rodríguez authorized Mass and the Sacrament of Penance to be celebrated in the church during construction and ordered work to resume during his pastoral visit on 17 August. On 25 January 1890, work stopped when senior officer Ricardo Pérez and architect Zapata retired without notice, and José María Zapata Muñoz resigned on 6 February, when the portico and dome collapsed. At a meeting on 15 February, the board accepted Zapata’s resignation, attributing the collapse to either structural design flaws or construction interruptions. The community blamed those in charge, leading to a public meeting on 17 February 1890 where all members resigned, though the villagers urged them to stay, and they ultimately retained their positions. The board then met two days later to assess the situation, appoint an architect to examine the structure, determine what needed to be demolished, and take charge of the work. Zapata never returned to Yarumal. The frame of the church was designed by Victoriano Palacio and reviewed on 21 May 1894 by Tomás Vásquez, who found it satisfactory. However, due to the collapse, the board commissioned an engineer review. Heliodoro Medina was assigned to find the engineer, who hired Heliodoro Ochoa to evaluate the project. On 10 August 1894, a well-attended meeting was held, and Ochoa recommended not building the portico due to stability concerns. The board and townspeople agreed, and Ochoa was hired to design the front face of the building. Ochoa later proposed roofing the rear of the church with wood instead of the original stone dome, a proposal approved by majority vote. After this, Ochoa examined the previous work and found the carpentry and masonry to be stable. On 21 February 1895, work stopped again due to lack of funds and difficulties in collecting contributions. Only masons continued working at half speed, storing materials until work resumed. All board members were asked to resign on that date, and construction remained practically paralyzed from 4 August 1895. The board ordered the church condemned on 12 October 1895. Father Ildefonso Tirado began holding religious ceremonies in the new church on 11 May 1899 to encourage donations, coinciding with the start of the Thousand Days War. In February 1900, wooden grilles for stained glass windows were begun. On 27 December 1900, the board authorized Díaz to begin work on the bell tower. On 15 February 1901, construction began on the wooden side doors; the main door started on 20 July 1903. On 20 May 1901, the Daughters of María installed the altar of the Immaculate Conception, commissioned with board approval in 1898. Heliodoro Ochoa was brought back to Yarumal from Medellín to continue work on the bell tower and buildings, and along with Juan Nepomuceno Gómez, worked on the latches. On 22 July 1901, Victoriano Palacio was chosen to direct the tiling of the church. Work stalled until July 1903, when it resumed after the visit of Bishop Manuel Antonio López de Mesa. By then, Victoriano Palacio had been commissioned to install the altar, work on the chancel molding, create two holy water fonts, and build the bell tower. However, the bishop realized the work had only resumed due to his visit and blamed both the war and the board, leading him to remove all board members and appoint a new one. He also recognized that Yarumal needed two churches due to its population and importance, and ordered the new board to focus on both the new church and maintenance of the cemetery chapel. According to Ochoa’s calculations, the dome required 210 large planks, 700 small planks, 12 hundredweights of copper, and 2 of tin. On 22 November, the board approved José María Hoyos’s proposal to install a temporary altar with the image of Saint Joseph in a side nave. On 6 January 1906, it was agreed to begin tiling the building. In the same meeting, Carlos Mejía Vargas, supported by other doctors, recommended moving all religious ceremonies to the old cemetery chapel due to health concerns, and the priest agreed. In June 1908, structural problems in one of the towers became evident, prompting Ochoa to provide advice from Medellín to reinforce it with wood. Ochoa arrived in Yarumal on 24 December and visited the site with the full board. The board followed all recommendations except those to remove the bells, believing the tower modifications provided sufficient support. On 21 April 1914, priest Leónidas Lopera Roldán ordered construction of the atrium under the direction of José López and Jesús María Saldarriaga, with designs by Joaquín Pinillos. The following year, Roldán commissioned the altar, which served as the main altar for many years, from craftsmen in Carvajal. On 5 February 1917, Pope Benedict XV issued the papal bull Quod catholicae, creating the Diocese of Santa Rosa de Osos, splitting the former Diocese of Antioquia, and making Yarumal part of the new diocese. On the night of 4 February 1938, an earthquake caused serious damage, including wall damage, settlement of the main arch’s foundation, and cracks in the apse. Father Gerardo Martínez Madrigal requested technical advice from architects and engineers, who conducted photographic studies. Evaluations varied, with some recommending iron reinforcement, others suggesting demolition and a new concrete arch with columns. The pastor chose to rebuild damaged portions brick by brick using the recommendations of Jesús Mejía. After repairs, Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes consecrated the Church of Our Lady of Mercy on 11 February 1944. In 1947, Father Francisco Gallego Pérez purchased the first organ for the church, a Hammond organ for 7,000 pesos, delivered on 16 July and blessed on 14 September. Efraím Jiménez, priest from 9 March 1953 to 24 March 1968, hired Raúl Bohórquez to decorate the towers with nickel silver. Jiménez also obtained the current marble altar, consecrated on 7 June 1955 by Builes, and bought the current church organ from Walcker Orgelbau of Ludwigsburg, Germany for 102,000 pesos. The Hammond organ was later sold for 25,000 pesos to the Chapel of the Theological Seminary of Santa Rosa de Osos. Meanwhile, the cemetery chapel began to deteriorate, and in 1992, Father Luis Enrique Restrepo Muñoz established a board to restore it as a historical site. On 23 November 1998, the Municipal Council of Yarumal declared the Church of Our Lady of Mercy and the Chapel of Saint Luis architectural landmarks. On 12 August 1999, under the leadership of Father Gilberto Melguizo Yepes, the temple was granted the title of Lower Basilica. The consecration was performed in a ceremony chaired by Bishop Jairo Jaramillo Monsalve. Yepes ordered the replacement of a fallen church lamp, obtained stained glass windows, three new bells, a new baptismal font, and the picture of Blessed Mariano of Jesús Euse Hoyos. He restored marble tiles in the temple, which were in terrible condition. Additionally, in an initiative by Yepes and the Municipal Council of Culture, in August 2000, the remains of poet Epifanio Mejía were moved from the San Pedro Cemetery to the basilica.

doc_name: Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Yarumal)
text: The Church of Our Lady of Mercy in Yarumal, built in the Renaissance Revival style, is a historicist structure primarily developed in the 19th and 20th centuries, featuring a rectangular floor plan with three longitudinal naves—main and two lateral—crossed by a transept that projects slightly but does not form a cruciform. The intersection of the transept and central nave supports a dome. The building has a symmetrical main façade facing the Epifanio Mejía Park, composed of two domed towers joined by a section framing the central nave, with three entrances—one central and two on the sides—each aligned with a nave. The side view reveals the towers, then the naves (with lateral naves lower than the central one), followed by the transept wall at the same height as the central nave, topped by the dome. The roof is tiled in clay, with gabled roofs on the central nave and transept and single-slope roofs on the lateral naves. The interior includes areas beneath the towers and choir loft, separated by walls, each containing Stations of the Cross paintings. The central nave is wider and taller, flanked by arcades of seven pillars each with square bases, shafts, and capitals, supported by semicircular arches; above, there is a wide decorative entablature with two series of six windows on each side, and a dropped ceiling with three large glass lamps. The transept is square, with corner pillars supporting an eight-window raised dome; lateral naves are nearly the same length as the central nave, have two series of six windows with decorative cornices, and include four Stations of the Cross paintings and two wooden confessionals. The southern side wall has a door, and the left wall connects to the chapel of the Fallen Christ, which links to the corridor of ossuaries and stairs to the towers and high chorus. The transept opens east–west, has the same width and height as the central nave, and features a marble railing and three steps leading to the main area, with additional steps near the presbytery emphasizing the altar. Niches in the transept walls contain images and windows; the baptismal font is in the western transept, with a niche in the north wall housing a high relief of the baptism of Jesus and a Chi Rho above it. The presbytery, elevated by seven steps, has a vaulted apse and includes the altar in a half baldachin, the table of sacrifice, the priest’s seat, and the ambon—all in marble. The reserve altar is a rectangular room four steps above, located at the end of the right nave. The basilica is constructed primarily of solid brick, with some side walls in rammed earth, both plastered internally and externally, with simulated block sizes. Bricks are held with lime mortar (calcium oxide, sand, water), which dries into a hard substance but is less resistant and impermeable than cement; cement was used after the 1938 earthquake. The façades are load-bearing, averaging 80 cm in thickness, with square-based nave pillars measuring 100 cm per side, and a stone foundation supported by brick. The roof is a wooden structure covered in clay tiles; the main dome is brick with a wooden structure and copper plates, and the tower domes are similarly constructed with copper plates appearing silver externally. The walls are tiled with multicoloured marble, similar in design to the Church of Nuestra Señora del Rosario, featuring marble inlays and fleurs-de-lis, with white marble terraces; the nave flooring uses coloured cement (hydraulic tile), common between the early and mid-20th century. During Father Gilberto Melguizo Yepes’ tenure, the marble tiling was restored after settling and sinking, with affected areas injected with grout and the paving polished to restore its appearance. The veneration of the Virgin of Mercy in Yarumal dates back to the founding of San Luis de Góngora in 1787, when the colonists declared her patron saint and protector, as recorded in a document from Medellín issued on 21 December 1787 by Visitor Juan Antonio Mon y Velarde. A painting of the Virgin of Mercy was commissioned in 1789 by Nicolás Valencia, a trader from Rionegro, and donated to the parish. It was solemnly installed in 1790 by Priest Nicolás Francisco Agudelos and confirmed as patron saint by Bishop Ángel Velarde y Bustamante on 27 January 1792. In 1915, Father Leónidas Lopera installed the image in the upper niche of a wooden altar; in 1930, Father Julio Ortega purchased a new frame and added protective glass. Gerardo Martínez Madrigal, before the Second Marian Congress in 1942, secured a hammered silver frame, shield, filigree brooch, and gold crown from Santa Fe de Antioquia, costing 950 pesos in labor and 2,000 pesos total, with the three gold items weighing 108 grams, the crown containing 24 gemstones and three pearls. The silver frame, weighing 11.5 kilograms, was donated by Yarumal women, with the top showing the Virgin of Mercy’s shield and the bottom in gold bearing the inscription "The parish of Yarumal of its exalted patron saint in the Second Marian Congress." On 28 August 1942, Father Francisco Galician Pérez removed the painting from its original frame to transfer it to the silver frame, discovering on the reverse a caption confirming Nicolás Valencia as the commissioner: "True portrait of the miraculous image of Our Lady of Mercy, redeemer of captives. A gift of Nicolás Valencia. Year 1789, a Hail Mary by the painter." On 23 September 1942, Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes blessed the jewels, which were then affixed to the painting and placed in the niche of honour in the 1915 wooden altar, with 3 mm glass installed for protection at a cost of 70 pesos. In 1987, during Yarumal’s bicentennial, the painting was canonically crowned by the Diocese of Santa Rosa de Osos and received the title "Perpetual Mayor of Yarumal"; in 1998, Monsignor Melguizo Yepes added a belt and gold sceptre. False legends, such as one claiming a traveler from Medellín left the painting at the "Contento" inn, are contradicted by historical records and the painting’s documented presence in the early church of San Luis de Góngora. The first altar was donated by the Salesian Sisters of Don Bosco in 1898 and installed on 20 May 1901. In 1915, Father Leónidas Lopera commissioned a wooden altar from Carvajal cabinetmakers, which served as the primary altar; due to the small size of the patron saint’s chapel, the image was placed outside the niche for visibility. A marble altar was later commissioned for the 1954 Marian year. Franco Lucarini of Marmolería Italiana de U. Luisi Eredi in Medellín was selected after receiving bids from masons in Medellín, Italy, and Bogotá. The church signed the agreement on 19 February 1954 and extended the contract on 10 June to include tiling of the presbytery and side chapel for 25,300 pesos. The unveiling was planned for 15–20 September 1954 during the Marian Congress, but delays occurred due to strikes in Italy. Work was sent by sea: the first shipment left on 19 September 1954, taking 25 days and 10 days to clear customs and arrive in Yarumal; the final shipment left on 15 December. A total of 18 trips transported 184 boxes weighing 100,820 kilograms from Cartagena to Yarumal, at a transport cost of 9,997.01 pesos. Assembly and placement began on 1 February 1955, with Manuel Rave Ángel and his son Gilberto hired for 16,000 pesos, as they had previously placed the marble altar from Santa Rosa de Osos in 1936. Before installation, the stone of the 1944 consecrated altar was removed, along with the relics of saints Teódulo, Martial, Modestina, and Amanda, to be placed in the new altar stone upon consecration.

doc_name: Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Yarumal)
text: It took 25 days to transport the altar components from Cartagena to Yarumal, with 10 days spent passing customs and arriving in Yarumal; the rest of the materials were sent by sea, with the final shipment departing on 15 December. A total of 184 boxes, weighing 100,820 kilograms, were transported in 18 trips from Cartagena to Yarumal, at a cost of 9,997.01 pesos. On 1 February 1955, work began to assemble and install the altar, with Manuel Rave Ángel and his son Gilberto hired for 16,000 pesos, considered ideal due to their prior work placing the marble altar from Santa Rosa de Osos in 1936. Before installation, the altar stone from the 1944 consecrated altar and the relics of saints Teódulo, Martial, Modestina, and Amanda were removed and stored in a metal box, sealed with the episcopal seal of Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes, who transferred them to the parish priest. Construction of the altar’s foundation began on 7 February 1955, made of metre-thick concrete; lifting of the eight three-tonne columns started on 19 February and was completed on 26 February. On 2 March, the capitals were installed on the columns, the 17th entablature (including architrave, frieze, and cornices) was placed, and five medallions representing the Four Evangelists and titular saint Aloysius Gonzaga were added; the cross was placed on 31 March. The altar rails were completed on 19 April, the altar of the Blessed Saint was ready on 21 April with a Venetian mosaic of Leonardo da Vinci’s The Last Supper, the shrine was finished on 28 April, and the painting of the Virgin of Mercy was set in the niche on 30 April. The altar was consecrated on 8 June 1955 by Bishop Builes, accompanied by clergy, the Seminar of Missions, and priest Efraím Jiménez, during a two-hour ceremony when the relics were placed in the new altar stone. On 10 April 1955, Antonio Boroughs Rendón of Medellín was contracted for 1,600 pesos to build an indirect lighting system; the church also purchased a red rug for greater splendour. On 24 August 1955, the wooden altar in the reserve chapel was removed and replaced with the 1915 altar, carried out by Eugenio Salazar between 26 August and 3 September, though the altar table remained in place due to deterioration. After the liturgical reforms of the Second Vatican Council, which ended the practice of celebrating mass with the priest facing away from the congregation, priest Roberto Arroyave Vélez needed the "Altar of the Sacrifice," also made of marble and consecrated by Bishop Ordóñez, which occurred on 18 September 1970. The altar is 12 metres (39 ft) high, 7 metres (23 ft) wide at the base, weighs 70 tonnes (77 short tons), and cost $23,000; it features eight monolithic columns, each 6 metres (20 ft) and 55 centimetres (22 in) in diameter, arranged in two semicircular rows, with Corinthian style matching the church’s architecture. The semicircular entablature rests on the capitals and includes an east-facing semi-dome with high relief ornaments, a central shield bearing the "I.H.S." monogram of Jesus Christ, and a cross at the top; at the base of the semi-dome are five medallions representing Aloysius Gonzaga and the Four Evangelists on a Venetian mosaic background. The half-dome and columns form a canopy sheltering the altar, the church tabernacle, a green marble shrine for the Virgin of Mercy with a monogram and ducal crown, the throne of the saint, and a reproduction of Leonardo da Vinci’s The Last Supper in Venetian mosaic. Interest in acquiring a musical instrument for religious celebrations began in 1880 when Father Aldemar Palacio received a letter from Jesús María Rodríguez, Provisor of the Bishop of Antioquia, ordering all churches in the diocese to have an organ; due to construction-related economic difficulties, the purchase was postponed. On 11 October 1900, Presbyter Emigdio A. Palacio requested the purchase of a musical instrument, and the Board of Manufacture agreed to contribute 1,000 pesos, up to 1,500 pesos if the organ was purchased. In 1947, Presbyter Francisco Galician Pérez bought a Hammond organ for 7,000 pesos, unveiled on 16 July by teacher Cabral and blessed by the parish priest on 14 September. The current pipe organ was obtained by priest Efraím Jiménez from Oskar Binder & Cia. Ltda. of Bogotá, the exclusive Colombian representative for E.F. Walcker of Ludwigsburg, Germany, founded in 1785 and experienced in building organs for tropical climates. A delegate from the firm visited Yarumal to assess the church’s style and acoustics, recommending a pipe organ with 17 registrations (1,020 pipes) valued at 102,000 pesos to be paid over three years. Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes approved the contract, congratulating priest Jiménez. The agreement was signed on 19 February 1961 by Presbyter Jiménez, Benedicto Soto Mejía, and Oskar Binder. The organ, weighing four tonnes, was shipped from Bogotá via Sonsón on 6 March 1963, arriving in Yarumal three days later and installed through the "Door of the Pardon"; installation began on 11 March, overseen by Oskar Binder, and the organ debuted on 19 March, the Day of Saint Joseph. It was blessed from the pulpit by Bishop Builes before the Sunday liturgy on 24 March. The Hammond organ was sold to the Chapel of the Conciliar Seminary of Santa Rosa de Osos for 25,000 pesos. The E.F. Walcker organ has 17 stops across two manual keyboards (61 keys each) and a pedal keyboard for bass, all in a console facing the altar; it controls 1,020 pipes of varying length and calibre. It functions as an orchestra with trumpets, bombards, oboes, clarinets, flutes, and human voices, made of varnished and sealed mahogany, powered by an electrical fan and a 14-volt dynamo. Of the 32 organs in Antioquia, the basilica’s is the eighth largest in area and volume. Early representations of Jesus’ passion and death were 50 x 60 cm oil paintings obtained by Bárbara Palacio of Mejía, aunt of Father Benedicto Soto, donated to the parish and later given to the chapel of the Pontifical Seminar of Missions, canonically erected by J. Buenaventura Marín on 7 October 1903 with Emigdio Palacio and vicar witnessing. The current Stations of the Cross paintings, made in 1945 and 1946, were commissioned by Francisco Galician Pérez to Mariela Ochoa U. of Medellín, copied from illustrations brought by Father Gallego from Germany, each costing 100 pesos. The church initially had simple stained glass windows; Monsignor Melguizo Yepes commissioned artistic stained glass from an artist in Cali using cathedral glass. There are 11 windows in total, covering the lower series between the transept and towers; the rest remain simple. Five stained glass windows face the Rosenda Torres school from north to south: Jesus with apostles, Saint Francis Xavier, Pope John Paul II (who beatified Father Mariano and granted the church the title of lower basilica), Mariano de Jesús Euse Hoyos (blessed and born in Yarumal, coadjutor), and Saint Joseph. Six windows face the eastern nave from north to south: Baby Jesus and Holy Family, the Good Shepherd, the birth of Jesus, the Trinity, the gubernatorial decree declaring the Virgin of Mercy perpetual mayor of Yarumal, and a replica of the Quiteño painting of the Virgin of Mercy. The central nave has four large crystal chandeliers, 3.2 metres (10 ft) high and 2.3 metres (7.5 ft) wide, purchased and installed between 1959 and 1960 by Presbyter Efraím Jiménez after a demonstration by a lamp seller. Two chandeliers were initially ordered as a trial; the first was permanently installed on 23 October 1959. The plan, finalized that year, included two more chandeliers in the central nave and smaller ones for Easter 1960 in the presbytery, reserve altar, side naves, and under the basilica’s dome, totaling 13 chandeliers ordered from French firm Baccarat at 60,000 pesos; the final chandelier was installed on 11 February 1960. On 2 December 1882, during construction, José María Díaz donated the first clock, originally installed in the tower above the "Door of the Pardon," moved to the circular area between windows on the central door in 1920. It remained until 24 May 1966, when it was replaced by a new four-faced clock from Vitoria, Spain, solemnly blessed by Bishop Builes the day before installation, with plans to place the old clock in the cemetery of Carmen. The clock rings every fifteen minutes using its own bells, activated by ropes that pull hammers to strike the bell. The original bells were in poor condition due to cracks reducing volume; Monsignor Melguizo Yepes arranged their replacement, removing the damaged ones from the right tower and sending them to the Tristancho workshops, a Colombian bellmaking dynasty with 250 years of history, where they were melted to create new bells using the lost mould technique. The process involves mixing three types of clay with horse manure, building a bamboo frame, layering the clay, and repeating the process; the interior and exterior are machined into bell shape, sheep tallow is applied to release the mould, a countermould is heated to absorb the tallow, and both are burned, leaving a cavity filled with molten copper and tin. The foundry uses mud ovens with dry firewood, melting the metal at 1,200 degrees Celsius; each bell is made in one piece and takes only three seconds to fill a mould for a 300 kg bell, then cools for two days before hand-polishing. The three new bells are large, bronze, and cost 7,500,000 pesos; unveiled by Melguizo in 1997, they were baptized from highest to lowest as the Lady of Mercy (500 kg), Saint Aloysius Gonzaga (310 kg), and Benedicto (300 kg), used to announce religious events and operated manually via ropes from the tower’s lower part. The church has had four baptismal fonts: the first in what is now the chapel of the Fallen Christ, formerly the baptistry, decorated with the Holy Trinity; the second built by Gallego Pérez, placed equidistant between the chapel of the Fallen Christ and the chapel of Our Lady of Perpetual Help; the third located in the left nave, constructed in 1975 by Father Roberto Arroyave from bogotana sandstone under the signature "Enchapes Sacatín" for 80,000 pesos; the fourth and current font is in the same location, acquired by Gilberto Melguizo Yepes, built from marble with a staggered octagonal base, square pillar, and octagonal basin. Two holy water fonts were purchased in 1945 by Father Ernesto Acosta Arteaga from Marmolería Artistica of Hermenegildo Bibolotti, each 160 centimetres (63 in) high, with base, column, basin, and a central angel statue. In 1924, Presbyteries Rafael and José Manuel Yepes Carvajal donated 12 large French candelabras (1.5 metres high) used during eucharistic vigils from 6 June to 16 July, concluding with the Virgin of Carmen celebration; Presbytery Luis Enrique Restrepo Muñoz restored them during his first five years; they remain mostly at the foot of the main altar. The basilica originally had a pulpit made by the Carvajales Martínez, finished with imitation marble and allegorical depictions of the evangelists, which was demolished on 25 January 1971; the rosettes are preserved in the Traditional Museum of Monsignor Juan N. Rueda. Before the Second Vatican Council, the church had a wide variety of art; these were removed on 18 July 1967 due to council provisions. Among the removed works were paintings of the Holy Family, Sacred Heart, Immaculate Heart of Mary, Saint Joseph, Saint John Eudes, Saint Roch, Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Saint Tarcisius, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, Infant Jesus of Prague, Infant Jesus of the Small Flock, the ancient Quiteño painting of the Virgin of Our Lady of Sorrows and Child Mary. Some remained temporarily, including the patron saint Our Lady of Mercy, titular saint Aloysius Gonzaga, Our Lady of Perpetual Help, the three pictures of the Ordeal, Our Lady of Fátima, Saint Augustine of Hippo, Saint Antonio, the embrace of Saint Francis of Assisi, Saint Nicholas of Tolentino, the Fallen Christ, and the divine countenance. Some images remained under review for retention: the Virgin of Carmen, one of the Immaculate Conception (by Bartolomé Esteban Murillo), Christ the King, and the Stations of Christ.

doc_name: Basilica of Our Lady of Mercy (Yarumal)
text: The paintings of the Holy Family, the Sacred Heart, the Immaculate Heart of Mary, Saint Joseph, Saint John Eudes, Saint Roch, Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, Saint Tarcisius, Our Lady of Mount Carmel, the Infant Jesus of Prague, the Infant Jesus of the Small Flock, the ancient Quiteño painting of the Virgin of Our Lady of Sorrows and the Child Mary were removed from the church on 18 July 1967. Some of these images, including the patron saint Our Lady of Mercy, the titular Saint Aloysius Gonzaga, Our Lady of Perpetual Help, the three pictures of the Ordeal, the Our Lady of Fátima, Saint Augustine of Hippo, Saint Antonio, the embrace of Saint Francis of Assisi, Saint Nicholas of Tolentino, the Fallen Christ, and the divine countenance, remained for a time before being removed. Other images, such as the Virgin of Carmen, one of the Immaculate Conception (by Bartolomé Esteban Murillo), Christ the King, and the pictures of the Stations of Christ, were still under determination for retention or removal; the final placement of the Stations of Christ was decided on 14 August 1967 based on the considerations of the parish priest and Bishop Félix María Torres Parra. The current images in the church are located in the transept: the Immaculate Conception, the Virgin of Carmen, Saint Francis of Assisi embracing Christ on the cross, the Sacred Heart of Jesus, Saint Joseph, and the Blessed Mariano de Jesús Euse Hoyos. The painting of the Fallen Christ is in the chapel, and at the reserve altar are the paintings of Mary Help of Christians, Salvator Mundi, and six angels. The early church of Yarumal originally had the image of the Christ on the Column, noted in the 1845 inventory, but today its details and current location are unknown. Due to the absence of a Passion scene, in 1935 Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes ordered the rector to commission the Fallen Christ image. Presbyter Gerardo Martínez Madrigal began preparations for the chapel adjacent to the presbytery, and on 10 September 1938 made the final payment to Misael Osorio. The statue of the Fallen Christ was carved by Constantino Carvajal in 1935 for 400 pesos, and the corresponding urn was made by Francisco Gómez Estrada for 100 pesos. The image was inaugurated on days celebrating the Eucharistic Congress and the patron saints and is currently located in a chapel at the foot of the temple, previously the baptistry, next to the left nave. Fernando Ramírez and his wife Elena Rivera, from Sopetrán, acquired in the late 19th century a Barcelonan picture of the Dormition of the Mother of God. Upon the death of their daughter Carmen Ramírez Rivera of Botero on 22 March 1955, her brother Germán Ceballos Ramírez transferred the image to the parish. The Assumption of Mary, symbolizing the elevation of Mary’s body and soul to heaven, originated in the apostolic period and was formally established as dogma by Pope Pius XII on 1 November 1950. This image arrived in Yarumal on 6 January 1963, carved by Josué Giraldo Mejía, and depicts three invocations: the Infant Mary, the Immaculate Heart of Mary, and Our Lady of the Rosary. It features blue clothing without a mantle, a rosary in her hands, a garland of pink roses symbolizing the joyful mysteries, a crown of red roses around her heart representing the painful mysteries, and a third crown of yellow roses around her feet symbolizing the glorious mysteries. On the night of 8 to 9 January 1958, a fire in the altar stone destroyed the crucifix; a new one was donated by Antonio Hoyos Mejía. The cross was crafted in Yarumal by cabinetmaker Alfonso Areiza Medina for 20 pesos, and artist David Pérez of Medellín created the Christ sculpture for 300 pesos. The work was delivered on Holy Thursday, 3 April of that year, and unveiled on Good Friday for public veneration. Christ is depicted carrying the three powers of gold from the Divine Boy Jesus of Prague, donated by Mercedes Ramírez Rivera. The cross has a glow produced by a copper encasement ordered by rector Roberto Arroyave, designed to imitate the image of the Lord of the Miracles, a crucifix in the Basilica of San Pedro of the Miracles. In the basilica, three masses are celebrated Monday through Saturday, and eight on Sundays; schedules may vary due to celebrations of the patron saint, Holy Week, Christmas, or the Catholic calendar.
